Untimely
ŭn-tīm´lĭ
adj. (before the due season; of a birth or a fig that drops unripe — Hebrew nephel; Greek olunthos)
From un- and timely. The Hebrew nephel is from the verb to fall — a birth that falls before its time; the Greek olunthos is the unripe winter fig that drops when the tree is shaken.

Biblical Definition

Untimely means before the appointed season, and Scripture uses it of two things that fall too soon. Of a birth: Job, in the depth of his misery, wishes he had been “as an hidden untimely birth… as infants which never saw light” (Job 3:16); the Psalmist prays against the wicked, “like the untimely birth of a woman, that they may not see the sun” (Psa 58:8); and the Preacher says that a man who has a hundred children and many years, whose soul is not filled with good and who has no burial, is worse off than an untimely birth (Ecc 6:3). In every case the phrase carries a weight of grief that Scripture does not minimize. Of fruit: at the sixth seal, “the stars of heaven fell unto the earth, even as a fig tree casteth her untimely figs, when she is shaken of a mighty wind” (Rev 6:13). Anyone who has seen a fig tree in a gale knows the picture — the small hard winter figs come down all at once, in a shower, because they were never fastened. That is John's image for the shaking of the heavens: what looked fixed comes down like unripe fruit when the wind rises.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines untimely as happening before the natural time; premature; and as an adverb, before the natural time.

expand to see more

UNTI'MELY, a. Happening before the natural time; premature; as untimely fruit; an untimely death.

UNTI'MELY, adv. Before the natural time.

PREMATU'RE, a. Ripe too soon; too early; happening or performed before the proper time.

FIG, n. The fruit of the fig tree; the winter or untimely fig, which drops unripe.

Key Scripture

Revelation 6:13 — "And the stars of heaven fell unto the earth, even as a fig tree casteth her untimely figs, when she is shaken of a mighty wind."

Ecclesiastes 6:3 — "If a man beget an hundred children, and live many years, so that the days of his years be many, and his soul be not filled with good, and also that he have no burial; I say, that an untimely birth is better than he."

Job 3:16 — "Or as an hidden untimely birth I had not been; as infants which never saw light."

Psalm 58:8 — "As a snail which melteth, let every one of them pass away: like the untimely birth of a woman, that they may not see the sun."

Modern Corruption

Grief that God recorded without rebuke is treated as unbelief, and the reader is left with no permission to say what Job said.

expand to see more

Job 3 is one of the darkest chapters in the Bible: a righteous man cursing the day of his birth and wishing he had been an untimely birth that never saw light. God preserved it in Scripture, and when He finally answered Job out of the whirlwind, He did not rebuke him for that chapter — He rebuked the friends who had spoken of Him wrongly, and told them to ask Job to pray for them. A church that permits its people no lament has less room in it than the Bible does. The Psalms are full of the same speech, and Christ Himself prayed one of them from the cross.

Ecclesiastes 6:3 measures a life by an unexpected standard. A hundred children and a long span, and yet a soul not filled with good and no burial at the end — and the Preacher says an untimely birth is better. That is a verdict on the accumulation of years and offspring and estate without God; the length is not the measure. Revelation 6:13 supplies the counterpart at the scale of the cosmos. When the mighty wind comes, what falls first is what was never firmly attached, and it falls all at once. The question the image asks a reader is not when the shaking comes but what he is fastened to.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew nephel (H5309), an untimely birth, from naphal, to fall — Job 3:16, Psalm 58:8, Ecclesiastes 6:3; Greek olunthos (G3653), the unripe winter fig — Revelation 6:13 only.

expand to see more

Hebrew nephel (H5309) — an untimely birth; Job 3:16, Psalm 58:8, Ecclesiastes 6:3, its only three occurrences.

Hebrew naphal (H5307) — to fall; the root, so the noun names a falling before the season.

Greek olunthos (G3653) — the unripe fig of winter; Revelation 6:13, its only occurrence.

Greek seio (G4579) — to shake; the mighty wind that brings the figs down.

Job 42:7-8 records that God's anger was kindled against the friends, not against the man who spoke Job 3.

Usage

"“As a fig tree casteth her untimely figs” — what was never fastened comes down first."

"“An untimely birth is better than he” — length is not the measure of a life."

"God preserved Job 3 in Scripture and did not rebuke it."
